item.title: Nation builds up resilience to push growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
Nation builds up resilience to push growth Experts hail sustained measures to boost domestic demand, rebalance economy China's ongoing effort to pivot on growth driven by domestic demand is strengthening its economic resilience and supporting global economic stability, while creating fresh opportunities for international businesses, said economists and executives. Their comments come amid a renewed debate over China's growth model, with critics arguing that excessive reliance on exports and constraints on domestic demand, especially consumption, could leave the Chinese economy vulnerable to external shocks, with potential repercussions for the global economy. Economists noted that such arguments overlook China's proactive measures to rebalance its economy, underestimate Chinese consumers' purchasing power and overstate the nation's exposure to global geoeconomic uncertainties, as its vast domestic market provides a buffer against external shocks and a stable foundation for growth. David Blair, US economist and author of the book How Nations Succeed: The China Case Study, said contrary to certain perception that China has done little to boost consumption, the country's success in raising real wages of its people has tremendously strengthened household purchasing power. According to Blair's calculations, China's median real wage — adjusted for inflation to reflect real income growth — has roughly increased ninefold since 2000, while that of the United States has seen no increase since 1979. The significant income growth has underpinned a substantial level of domestic consumption in China, which is easily underestimated due to exchange rate factors and differences in consumption behavior between China and the West, he said. Statistics from the National Bureau of Statistics show that China's domestic consumption and investment accounted for more than 80 percent of its 4.7 percent GDP growth in the first half of 2026, indicating that domestic demand continued to be the main driver of growth. Luo Zhiheng, chief economist at Yuekai Securities, said that China's large domestic market serves as a strong buffer against external shocks. China's resilient economic growth, backed by a vast domestic market, still outpaces that of many other major economies and continues to uphold the nation's status as a key stabilizer of the global economy, Luo added. Looking ahead, analysts said there remains considerable room for China to further strengthen the role of domestic consumption in powering growth, with untapped potential for spending on services, and in rural areas and western China. With the right policies, this potential could translate into more resilient and sustainable economic growth, rather than a source of vulnerability, they said. Xiong Yi, chief economist for China at Deutsche Bank, said the Chinese government has been taking proactive steps to ramp up consumer spending in the services sector. "A key measure is cash handouts to families raising children, which began last year. This is a long-term policy, and the benefits could potentially be increased in the future," he said. "With these supportive government policies both on the supply side and demand side, we see services spending becoming a longer-term driver for consumer spending; not just for this year, but for the next five to 10 years," Xiong added. Policy efforts to unlock consumption potential are continuing. Starting on Sunday, China will broaden access to housing provident fund savings, allowing withdrawals for home renovations and property management fees and easing conditions for rental payments — a move analysts said will help spur housing-related spending. The Ministry of Finance extended interest subsidies to all categories of new credit card installment transactions starting on Aug 1, lowering financing costs to support household spending. Zhang Lupeng, a senior official at the National Development and Reform Commission, said China has distributed 187.5 billion yuan ($28 billion) of its 250 billion yuan allocation for consumer goods trade-ins this year and will expedite plans for extending consumer goods trade-in policies into 2027. Foreign businesses are enjoying the perks. Iris Cui, vice-president of Asia procurement and operations at Apple, said the company has benefited from trade-in incentives covering smartphones, tablets and smartwatches, as domestic and foreign brands are treated equally. Dave Ernsberger, president of S&P Global Energy, said, "China has the potential to generate tremendous demand and innovation, creating broad benefits, as its domestic market expands rapidly." Economists, nevertheless, emphasized the need to further scale up pro-consumption measures, flagging the slowdown of consumer spending this year amid prolonged property market weakness. Data from the NBS shows that in the first eight months, retail sales grew 1.1 percent year-on-year, compared with 4.6 percent for the same period in 2025. In August alone, the growth in retail sales slowed to 0.4 percent. Luo, from Yuekai Securities, attributed the headwinds facing consumption growth to property sector adjustments and the transition of growth drivers. The property downturn has weighed on purchases of home appliances, furniture and renovation services, he said, noting that falling home values have constrained households' willingness and ability to spend while debt burdens remain. Emerging industries are more technology- and capital-intensive, rather than labor-intensive, and thus provide less direct support for employment, he added. Raising household incomes should be the top priority to boost consumption, said Luo, who proposed channeling more State-owned capital gains into social security funds, encouraging listed companies to pay higher dividends and establishing a special guiding fund offering incentives for companies to raise workers' wages. Luo also underlined the need for stronger macroeconomic policy support, including interest rate cuts and expanded government bond issuance, during the rest of the year. A meeting of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee in July announced that pragmatic and effective incremental policies will be introduced in a timely manner, and it urged intensified efforts to step up countercyclical adjustments, expand domestic demand and optimize supply. US economist Blair said that raising the real wages of median workers would be indispensable for maintaining China's growth miracle in the coming decades. "The only legitimate way to increase people's spending (power) is by increasing their wages," he said, adding that other ways, such as creating asset bubbles and relying excessively on entitlements, would be deleterious in the long run. Liu Zhihua and Jiang Xueqing contributed to this story. Contact the writers at zhoulanxv@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Jiayu upscaling cabbage farming
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
Jiayu upscaling cabbage farming With the continuous work of generations of agricultural scientists, a domestically bred cabbage variety has not only helped Jiayu county in Central China's Hubei province reduce its reliance on imported seeds, but has also made it a fine example of the integration of agricultural innovation and industrial development. The county in Xianning has 180,000 mu (12,000 hectares) producing 720,000 metric tons of cabbage a year, local statistics show. Its efforts to strengthen the industry begin with the seed. China has relied heavily on imported cabbage seeds since the 1980s. However, high prices and unstable supplies made it hard for farmers to increase their incomes, said Qiu Zhengming, chief scientist with the Hubei Academy of Agricultural Sciences. In 2008, Jiayu began working with the team of Fang Zhiyuan of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences to develop cabbage varieties more suited to local conditions. After 10 years of research, Zhonggan 1305, a variety bred for winter cultivation, was introduced in 2018 and has become a major winter cabbage variety in the Yangtze River basin. The variety covers nearly 100,000 mu in the county, accounting for 70 percent of its winter cabbage planting area. The county is also using digital tools to improve how vegetables are grown. At a vegetable science and technology demonstration park, a network of sensors monitors field temperature, humidity and pest activity around the clock. A digital platform helps standardize production, from raising seedlings to managing crops and harvesting, Qiu said. A linked QR code system also allows consumers to trace vegetables back to the plots where they were grown, he said. It is important to use technology to improve production, Qiu said, adding that the aim is to keep vegetables affordable for consumers while ensuring growers can make a profit. The industry also provides jobs for nearby villagers. At a local vegetable growing base, Pan Jin'e spends the busy September season transplanting cabbage seedlings. She can plant two mu and earn 220 yuan ($32.85) a day. The seedlings planted in mid-September will be ready for harvest by late November, she said. During peak vegetable planting season, over 30 workers like Pan were hired to transplant, weed and water crops, said Zhu Wenjing, head of the base. "Many nearby villagers take these jobs, and they can earn a steady income close to home," Zhu said. In 2025, Jiayu's vegetable planting area covered 460,000 mu and the county produced 1.36 million tons of vegetables, with an output value of 6.4 billion yuan, according to local statistics. In addition to supplying domestic markets, its vegetables were also sold to countries including South Korea, Japan and Russia. Ma Jiliang, a researcher at the Institute of Agricultural Economics and Development of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, said that Jiayu shows how scientific research can support local industries. Building a regional vegetable brand with a geographical indication depends on science and technology, he said, adding that varieties with independent intellectual property rights are key to the industry's competitiveness. China now accounts for more than half of global vegetable production and about 40 percent of consumption, Ma said, adding that the industry's focus is shifting toward better quality and higher returns. "For farmers, that means earning more from growing vegetables. And for consumers, it means having high-quality vegetables in their plates," he said.

item.title: The many ways we listen
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
The many ways we listen Four people share their experiences at an event that encourages everyone to engage more closely with each other, Chen Yuehua reports. A bowl of Henan hula tang (a peppery, savory breakfast soup), 622 wartime photographs, a soprano's voice, and a young British student's observations of China came together at a youth dialogue at Vision China in London on Thursday. Held under the theme "Listen to Each Other, Open New Horizons", the discussion brought four young people from different backgrounds to one conversation. Their stories showed how listening can begin with something deeply personal. For Marcus Detrez, listening begins with history. A Frenchman whose family was caught in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression from 1931 to 1945, Detrez has a personal connection to the war. Two of his grandfather's children were killed during the conflict, he said. In 2025, Detrez brought a collection of 622 historical photographs his grandfather took in China. The photographs provide firsthand evidence of the destruction and atrocities of the war and help preserve the memory of what happened. Yet Detrez was also struck by what appeared between the scenes of destruction. "Something that blew my mind is the capacity of Chinese people's perseverance. At the same time, they cherish the very simple, daily things," he said. He noticed people taking walks and sharing meals during the war. Those ordinary scenes, he said, reveal the perseverance of people living through extraordinary violence. The other speakers brought listening into everyday life. Liu Wenchao, a Nottingham graduate who opened London's first hula tang breakfast shop, spoke about bringing a taste of his Henan hometown to London. He missed the soup himself. Then, he began sharing it with others. He recalled German customers arriving at his shop at 6 am, even before him. For Liu, food gives strangers a reason to sit down and talk. He wants customers to taste something unfamiliar, ask questions, and discover the story behind it. A bowl of soup can become a small introduction to Henan and to the memories of the person serving it. Yan Zhaoyi, a young Chinese soprano and a PhD candidate at the University of Oxford, approaches cultural exchange through music. She said the Chinese language itself has a musical quality, and singing can help audiences feel the meaning behind the words. "Listening means hearing what the other person really needs," Yan said, "rather than constantly putting into them what you want them to hear." She also hopes Chinese opera can enter into dialogue with other musical traditions, from jazz to contemporary popular culture. At one point, she imagined a Peking Opera version of Harry Potter. Harry Reay Wood, a young British student and Chinese-language learner, shared another perspective. This summer, the "Chinese Bridge" Chinese Proficiency Competition for Foreign College Students gave him a prize, adding a fresh achievement to his growing connection to China. He said more young people around him are curious about China. "I think a big reason is social media algorithms," Wood said. "It's what they're consuming online, what they're seeing on TikTok and Instagram." He described his friends' reactions: "My friends send videos to me, and people at school are like, 'Oh my goodness, this is what China actually looks like. This is incredible. I did not expect it to look this cool. Let's go to China.'" Wood also pointed to China's visa-free policy for British and other European citizens as another reason that online curiosity can turn into an actual trip. The four speakers saw China as a place where tradition and modern life meet. For them, meaningful communication starts with curiosity and respect. That outlook also reflects a broader generational pattern. The Pew Research Center surveys in 2024, 2025 and 2026 found that in most countries surveyed, younger people tend to hold more favorable views of China than older people. From viral China travel videos to "Chinamaxxing", a trend of embracing aspects of Chinese life, young people are increasingly curious about what everyday life is like in China. For them, curiosity has turned into a desire to experience China firsthand. Contact the writer at chenyuehua@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: A bowl of lamb soup honors Red Army
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
A bowl of lamb soup honors Red Army In the heart of Anwen township, Chongqing's Qijiang district, a unique educational experience recently unfolded for 164 first-year middle school students, who embarked on a journey to a local revolutionary-themed site — the A Bowl of Lamb Soup Exhibition Hall. The historical site, deeply rooted in the legacy of the Long March, served as a living classroom where the students engaged in fieldwork to immerse themselves in the revolutionary history and culture of the area. "Visiting the site made history feel incredibly close to us, and we truly felt the bravery and selflessness of the revolutionary figures," said Jin Junjiang, a student from Anwen school, during the event in early September. The exhibition hall commemorates a poignant local legend from January 1935, when the Central Red Army passed through Yangjiao village in Qijiang during the Long March. Liu Weizhen, a local villager, had just given birth and was alone at home. Soldiers offered her lamb soup and a military coat, which not only comforted her but also encouraged villagers to return home from hiding. The Long March, a monumental expedition covering approximately 12,500 kilometers, was a pivotal event in Chinese history. It not only marked the Communist Party of China's strategic transfer but also exemplified the profound bond between the army and the people. That bond is now commemorated at the A Bowl of Lamb Soup Exhibition Hall, a tribute by the local community. Qijiang holds a significant place in history as the only location in Chongqing crossed by the Central Red Army during the Long March. Although the army's stay there lasted only eight days, the period is regarded as the prelude to the Zunyi Conference and the overture to the Four Crossings of the Chishui River — pivotal events that laid the foundation for the victory of the Long March. Eighty-six-year-old Wang Xianjin reflected on a family memory that has endured for decades: "This bowl of lamb soup is something my mother never forgot. She often said that without the kindness of the Red Army, poor families like us wouldn't have survived." The story, passed down by their mother, profoundly shaped Wang's whole family. Inspired by her tales of the Red Army, Wang and his two brothers joined the CPC at a young age. Since 2022, Wang has volunteered as a guide at the A Bowl of Lamb Soup Exhibition Hall, sharing the cherished tale of the Long March with visiting students, officials and tourists. Today, his elder brother, now 88, and his younger brother, 84, continue to promote the revolutionary spirit through nostalgic paintings, writings and speeches. "Even in our 80s, the three of us remain committed to upholding our integrity and carrying forward the spirit of the Long March," Wang said. Anwen lamb, a local breed documented since the late Ming and early Qing dynasties, has become a culinary hallmark of the region. Xu Lu, an official in Anwen, noted that local people have leveraged the area's revolutionary culture and established specialized cooperatives centered on Anwen lamb, exploring a new path for rural vitalization. Since 2020, the area has developed five main attractions, including historical sites and the exhibition hall, offering nostalgic activities such as straw weaving, oil pressing and rice cake making. These efforts have attracted more than 100,000 visitors, generating more than 400,000 yuan ($60,000) for the local economy and increasing residents' earnings by more than 10 million yuan.

item.title: Asian Games open in Nagoya after challenging build-up
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
Asian Games open in Nagoya after challenging build-up NAGOYA, Japan -- The 20th Asian Games opened in Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday after a challenging buildup marked by accommodation shortages, transportation problems, heavy rainfall and other logistical issues. Under the slogan "Imagine One Asia," the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games mark Japan's third time hosting the event, following Tokyo in 1958 and Hiroshima in 1994. Unlike previous Asian Games, Aichi-Nagoya did not build a traditional Athletes' Village. Instead, organizers opted to use existing hotels, a cruise ship and temporary container-style huts, citing cost control and a desire to avoid leaving behind underused infrastructure after the Games. The approach came under scrutiny as the number of participants rose beyond initial expectations. Organizers had originally planned accommodation for around 15,000 people, while the final number of athletes and officials approached 17,000. Some delegations reported delays in room allocations and credential activation, while concerns also arose from room assignments and the distance between accommodation and competition venues. The OCA defended the overall accommodation strategy, saying the priority was to provide athletes with suitable accommodation, transportation, food and other services while ensuring infrastructure investments remained useful after the Games. The final days before the opening were also affected by torrential rain in the Nagoya area, which disrupted transportation and led to evacuations in some areas. Some Games facilities were affected by water leaks, adding another challenge for organizers shortly before the ceremony. Against that backdrop, the opening ceremony provided a chance to shift the focus back to sport.

item.title: Cultivating deeper cultural bonds encouraged at event
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
Cultivating deeper cultural bonds encouraged at event Engagement with China fosters a deeper understanding of the country and encourages more people from abroad to visit China, meet its people and experience its culture, said experts in education, art and music on Thursday. They made the remarks during a Vision China event held at the global headquarters of the Institution of Civil Engineers in central London, the United Kingdom. The event, themed "Listen to Each Other, Open New Horizons", aimed to inspire its audiences to engineer a cultural bridge to overcome boundaries with an inclusive mindset. The London edition of Vision China followed a recent phone conversation between President Xi Jinping and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. It underscored their consensus on the importance of communication and exchanges in developing bilateral relations. During the phone call, Xi urged China and the UK to seek common ground while reserving differences and make their mutually beneficial cooperation even stronger. Burnham expressed the UK's readiness to advance bilateral cooperation across all fields and strengthen people-to-people exchanges. Qu Yingpu, publisher and editor-in-chief of China Daily, which hosted Thursday's event, said via video call that "by heeding this shared vision, China and the UK can also encourage the wider international community to bridge differences and work together". Even though advancements in technology have made communication quicker and easier, "we still need closer exchanges to break preconceptions that often shape how we see one another", Qu said. He called on everyone to see, meet and listen, in order to build better understanding through empathy and carry forward friendly relations. "We need to open new horizons for international cooperation and development, and make greater contributions to building a community with a shared future for humanity," Qu added. Zhao Fei, charge d'affaires ad interim of the Chinese embassy in the UK, also gave a speech. Ondrej Dostal, a member of the European Parliament representing Czechia, said that he has traveled to China several times and has seen how the nation has effectively become the world's most significant innovator and producer, which is more than mere technological prowess. For many people in the West, "perceptions have simply failed to keep pace with reality" and there is an "enormous gap between the real China and perceptions of China", he said, referring to the intentional smearing of China in Western political discourse and media, which is designed to prevent engagement with the country and contain its rise. "Therefore, a great deal of work is ahead of us in explaining China's vision to Europe and to the world," Dostal said, noting that Europe and China face "too many common challenges to allow misunderstandings to define our relationship". "Only when we see China as it actually is can Europe formulate a China policy based on reality, rather than projection. Only then can we move beyond outdated stereotypes and manufactured threat narratives. Only then can we move beyond rivalry and finally embrace partnership — and, I hope, friendship," he added. For renowned British Sinologist Frances Wood, mutual learning is not just a good-to-have, but also central to her 30 years of work at the British Library, which involves the conservation and digitization of some 7,000 complete manuscripts and 6,000 fragments of ancient scrolls from Dunhuang, Northwest China's Gansu province, dating from the third century to the 10th century. She recalled how British and Chinese conservators worked together to repair the fragments, forging friendships and a family-like bond along the way. "After decades of hard work, we had a lot to show for it — over 7,000 'new' manuscripts transformed from 'debris', and the publishing of a series of academic books," Wood said. For Chen Junyan, winner of the second prize at the Leeds International Piano Competition in 2024, listening is not a metaphor. "It is what we do," she said, adding that music education in Shanghai and London taught her that listening helps broaden one's horizons. She noted that one of her primary reasons for being a pianist is being able to play chamber music with instrumentalists from different countries. "When I play ... I listen. They respond. I change. They change. Eventually, we create something that none of us on stage could have created alone," Chen said. "Meaningful cultural exchanges work very much in the same way. It is about being curious enough to listen, and being confident enough to allow what we hear to change us." Mike Longhurst, a fellow of UK's Royal Photographic Society, said that he saw China through different lenses — as a photographer, a businessman, a tourist and a sustainability consultant — during his visits to different Chinese cities. He captured on camera the Pudong skyline from the Bund in Shanghai; the majestic Great Wall in Beijing; the ancient Terracotta Warriors in Xi'an, Shaanxi province; the giant pandas in Chengdu, Sichuan province; and the karst landscapes in Guilin, Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. "But what I loved most is seeing the people. It is the people and their values that determine how all things are created, maintained and presented. … I see a togetherness that is missing in many cultures," Longhurst said. "China is so vast that whatever I have seen can only be a very small part. I hope to go back again and see more," he added. As China extended its visa-free policy to many European countries, including ordinary British passport holders in February, more people from the UK and Europe are traveling to China to see the country with their own eyes. Meanwhile, China remains one of the UK's most important sources of visa applicants. The growth in people-to-people exchanges is even more pronounced in the field of education. Around 100,000 Chinese students visit the UK for higher studies each year. Richard Trainor, provost of Rhodes Trust at the University of Oxford, said the 44 Chinese Rhodes scholars to date have become central to its scholar community, which encompasses continents and disciplines. "Chinese Rhodes scholars show that empathy, collaboration and courage are key attributes for 21st century leadership," said Trainor. Michael Spence, president and provost of University College London, noted the contributions of UCL's 15,000 Chinese students and 30,000 Chinese alums, as well as the university's role in promoting Chinese language learning in public schools across England. "Shared language is, of course, only one route to building trust among many. Yet for me, it most clearly underlines the values needed for trust and cooperation," Spence said, recalling his own Chinese language studies. Listing some daunting global challenges — from fighting climate change to governing artificial intelligence — Spence said he does not see any "reasons for pessimism", because what British and Chinese students, scholars and researchers have already achieved through collaboration is "proof of what is possible". The Vision China event also included a dialogue session, in which six young panelists from China, the UK and France exchanged views on economic and trade cooperation, people-to-people exchanges and cultural interactions. Through candid sharing of ideas, they explored their experiences and perspectives across borders, contributing to greater understanding and common ground and highlighting the role that young people play in shaping the future of China-UK and China-Europe relations. Contact the writers at xingyi@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: 'Rabbit island' a dark outpost of Japan's chemical warfare
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
'Rabbit island' a dark outpost of Japan's chemical warfare Researchers, peace activists work to preserve history of poison gas use, urge Tokyo to acknowledge role as aggressor A short distance from Hiroshima, in Japan's Seto Inland Sea, lies Okunoshima, a small island where the Imperial Japanese Army once produced poison gas. More than 80 years ago, during the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45), the poison gas was sent to China for use as chemical weapons, causing heavy casualties. Rabbits, the original inhabitants of this island, were also harmed. About 200 were used for poison gas testing and killed after Japan's defeat. Those roaming the island today were introduced later to attract tourists. The island is now a popular tourist destination known as a "rabbit paradise", and home to roughly 1,000 of the furry mammals. In stark contrast to the global awareness of the atrocities inflicted by the atomic bombing of Hiroshima on Aug 6, 1945, Okunoshima's dark past remains little known. Japanese researchers and peace activists have called on Japan to move beyond a narrative centered on its own wartime suffering, and confront its history as an aggressor and the pain it inflicted on people in China and other Asian countries. They have also warned that the memory of Japan's wartime aggression risks fading as researchers and volunteer guides grow older.

95 years after '9.18 Incident': Japan's mask comes off Share - WeChat
The "9.18 Incident" marked the beginning of the Japanese militarist invasion of China and its broader aggression across Asia. In the first half of the 20th century, the people of China and other victimized Asian countries suffered immensely under Japanese militarism, enduring untold disasters and hardships. This history must be remembered — not only by those who suffered, but even more so by the Japanese themselves. Those who forget history are doomed to repeat it; those who ignore their guilt will surely stumble again. We remember not to perpetuate hatred, but to safeguard peace. We keep the warning bells ringing not to dwell on the past, but to caution the future.

item.title: A China-Arab art documentary unveiled
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
A timeless painting does more than depict a landscape—it tells a story. In the spring of 2026, the 14th "Silk Road: Artists' Rendezvous — Renowned Arab Artists Visit China for Cultural Exploration" brought together nine distinguished Arab artists from Egypt, Oman, Jordan, Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia for a cultural exploration in China. Alongside three Chinese painters, they embarked on a journey from Beijing's Forbidden City to the scenic mountains and seas of Fujian. Throughout their travels, they created art and built friendships, culminating in a collaborative scroll painting titled A Journey of Mountains and Seas, A Journey in Song, as well as individual masterpieces. This artistic expedition became a dialogue between civilizations, expressed through five distinct colors. Red: Echoes of ancient civilizations Egyptian artist Mohamed Sabry Bastawy Hassan chose red as the focal color of his work. From the majestic Forbidden City to the intricate art of glove puppetry, he found a shared spiritual essence. His piece, The Tree of Life, uses Chinese red to cleverly merge ancient Egyptian script with the Chinese auspicious number "eight". Blue: Maritime Silk Road resonance Omani artist Yousuf Ali Hamed Al-Nahwi employed deep blue to depict ancient sailing vessels. Blue serves as the foundation of his paintings, symbolizing beauty and spiritual solace. Through three paintings, he illustrates the maritime Silk Road connection between China and Arab countries, exclaiming with admiration, "China is incredible!" Yellow: A shared sense of home Jordanian artist Rania Hamad Mousa Albayaydah and Omani artist Maryam Mohamed Abdul Karim Al Zadjali were inspired by the warm yellow hues of Zhangzhou's tulou and Yunshuiyao Ancient Town. The wisdom of constructing tulou with raw earth parallels traditional Jordanian architecture. Rania captured the beauty of Eastern homes by depicting Chinese women, while Maryam's triptych, Harmony in Diversity, Beauty in Coexistence, links landmarks from six Arab countries with the Great Wall of China, celebrating the sentiment of "harmony in diversity". White: The philosophy of blank space Algerian artist Yasser Ameur delved into the significance of white in traditional Chinese ink painting. Guided by Chinese painter Zhang Qiuju in Fuzhou, he learned that "leaving blank space isn't emptiness; it's an invitation for imagination." The two artists exchanged paintings, forging a friendship across mountains and rivers. Green: A love letter to China Moroccan artist Sidi Mohammed Mansouri Idrissi named his work after the tour guide Luo Chen. The lush green tea mountains of Wuyi Mountain and the vitality of the younger generation inspired his heartfelt tribute: "I came from Morocco with brushes and canvas, thinking I would depict you, but found that you are reshaping me. My paintings all bow before your greatest masterpiece: China!"
